_what: The person's files files at the local door (src/account_files/account_routes.rs): at `resource`, each of `operations` is answered by the account files' tool of that name (src/account_files/mod.rs `call`, the hosted Worker's file contract: list_files {folder?, after?, limit?}, find_file / show_file {name_or_identity}, read_file {name_or_identity, offset?, length?, encoding?: auto, text when the bytes are UTF-8 and not an image, or base64, always base64}, files_summary {}, usage_days {after?, limit?} (the account's own usage day rows, src/account_files/usage.rs), write_file {name, text | content_base64, media_type?}; share_file {name_or_identity, seconds}, an address (`<origin>/share/<id>/<key>`) that GETs the file without other credentials for 1 up to 604800 seconds, whole or by byte range, as often as its holder likes until the share ends or the person stops it (the byte route src/share_bytes reads the person's share again on every request), kept as an @namespace/shares record, never the URL) or one of its generic name operations (src/account_files/names.rs: find_names {prefix, after?, limit?}, the names in the prefix's folder that start with it; move_names and copy_names {from, to, after?, limit?}, a name or a whole folder of names, at most `limit` steps a call, answering next_after until done; set_aside and put_back {name, after?, limit?}, a name or folder moved into the set-aside tree at the same full name and back; list_set_aside {folder?, after?, limit?}). Only name records change: a file and its bytes are never copied or deleted by them. forget_set_aside {name, after?, limit?} forgets a set-aside name or folder for good and notes each file for the byte release; retire_names {names: [{name, expected_identity, retire: true}]} sets aside and forgets owned temporary names by exact path and expected identity, answering {retired, repeated, conflicts} (src/account_files/names.rs). The byte release (src/account_files/release.rs): queue_release {limit?} turns noted files nothing holds into release rows and forgets their records; release_gone_bytes {limit?} claims those rows, removes each object from its store and reports it released, until the call's time ends; list_released {after?, limit?} pages the storage given back. Results kept about files (src/account_files/results.rs), by content identity and kind and found by any of the file's identities: record_file_results {results: [{identity, kind, value, produced_by?, only_if_absent?}]}; read_file_results {identity, kind?, caller?}; read_file_result_fields {identity, kind, fields, caller?}; list_file_results {kind?, after?, limit?, caller?} (no kind: the count of each kind); read_file_results_many {kind, identities, caller?}; merge_file_result {identity, kind, value, produced_by?, only_if_empty?}; remove_file_result {identity, kind}. A read past the caller's most open reads answers {busy, retry_after_seconds}. The account's files lives in its state folder in the file its resources are placed in (src/storage/record_store_resources.json, a record store the account files migration made); an account without one answers that its files is unavailable. Bytes are read and written through the account's origin records, signed by the account's secrets vault. `run_operations` are what a Workshop tool run may be granted here (invoke.records.rights[]: {files: "/" for every name, or a folder path ending in "/" for the names under it; operations}), each with its rule of what one call touches (account_rights/run_rules.rs): a call naming a name (`id`, each of them when it names two: a move's from and to) or a folder (`id_prefix`) is covered by a folder right when the name or folder is under it; a call naming a file by its identity, or the whole account files (files_summary), only by a right on every name. `run_outputs.folder` is where the files a finished Workshop run made are kept (src/tool_runs/tools/outputs.rs, for a row's invoke.outputs): `<folder>/<tool>/<run>/<file>`, written by the engine itself, so a tool needs no right here to have its output kept.

search._what: The words in the person's file names, searched with one question (src/account_files/mod.rs AccountFiles::search, the port of old trillion src/search.mjs:1364 `words-in-names`, the `file-names` lane of src/search.json). Input {question, limit?}: the question cut to `question_chars`, its distinct words of at least `min_word_length`; candidates are the files the record store word index holds (every text of a `@namespace/files` record is indexed at write time, its `names` among them) for every uncommon asked word (a word with `word_hits` postings narrows nothing), and a file is kept when every asked word starts a word of the last part of one of its names. Answers {question, terms, results: [{id, source, identity, name, path, title, media_type, byte_length, found_in, places, said, address: {resource, operation, input}, score}], unavailable, pending}; the score is `rank` over (`k` + the file's rank), the weight the old lane had, so a caller merges it with the records' answer (records-routes.json `search`) by rank: a Workshop tool does, as old trillion src/search.mjs:1750 `finish` did; the engine merges nothing. `limit` is 1..`most`.

_recent: The files the person used most recently and how (old trillion src/recent-files.mjs and src/recent-files.json, ported one to one onto account rows: src/account_files/recent.rs). A use is {file, kind}: `kind` matches `kind_pattern`, and `words` only says how a kind reads (a kind with no row reads as itself, first letter raised, dashes as spaces). The engine stamps the time. One row per file in `@account-files/recent/files` (id the file's identity) holding each kind's newest time, and one row per file in `@account-files/recent/order` whose id sorts newest first; at most `keep` files are kept, the one used longest ago leaving first. `uses` are the door operations that keep a use when they answer: a row's `operation` keeps `kind` for the file its input names (`file`, a name or identity), and `when_zero`, when set, keeps it only when that input field is absent or 0 (a read from the start, not every range after it). `recent_files {limit?, before?}` reads `list_default` (at most `list_max`) newest first, a renamed file by its name now, a file no longer kept left out; `record_file_use {file, kind}` keeps one use.
_facts: The facts kept about each file are its result of kind `kind` (old trillion src/file-tools.mjs:135 set_file_facts, the results merge of kind facts: POST /namespace/results/<identity>/merge {kind: 'facts', value: facts}). `set_file_facts {identity, facts, produced_by?}` is that merge (src/account_files/results.rs merge_file_result): only the facts it names change, null takes one away, the same facts again write nothing, and the facts are kept under whichever of the file's identities already holds them; it answers {identity, kept_under, kind, value, changed}. They are read back with read_file_results {identity, kind} like every other result, and bounded by `results.max_value_bytes`: one owner for every result, no second row.
_usage: The account's own usage counts (src/account_files/usage.rs): every flush_seconds the one flush thread adds each counted account's stored, read and worked counts to its day row in @namespace/usage, off every request path. usage_days {after?, limit?} reads those rows (a right on every name, as files_summary).
_folder: What a native folder on a device (the files core, tools/files-on-every-device) reads and writes here, beside the calls above (src/account_files/folder.rs). Every name and folder row that list_files, show_item and list_changes answer carries `item`, `version` and `generation`. `item` is the row's stable id, kept by the store as the row's minted column (src/store/tables.json `minted`): a new name or folder gets the store's change order of the change that made it; a move, a rename, set_aside and put_back carry it, so a rename is never a delete plus a create; a copy_names copy and a name made again after it was forgotten get a new one; a name written again with new bytes keeps it (its `identity` is the content version). `version` is the row's own version, the number every write's `expected_version` names (0: the name must not exist yet). `generation` is the store's change order of the row's last change: it only grows, across a rename too, and is the metadata revision a file browser asks for beside the content identity. list_files answers `folder_items` beside `folders`: for each child folder its {item, version, generation}. list_changes {after?, limit?, wait?, device?} answers {changes, next}: with no `after` it answers no changes and `next`, the cursor of now (read the tree with list_files, then follow changes from there); with `after` (a cursor this call answered) it answers the changes to the person's names and folders made after it, in the store's own order, at most `limit` (1 to the store's page bound, list_files' default when not given), and `next` to ask from. A change is {op, kind, item, generation} plus, for op `put`, the row as list_files answers it (name or folder and its facts); op `remove` means the item is in no live name any more (forgotten, or set aside into Recently Deleted, which list_set_aside reads). A rename answers one `put` of the item under its new name and no `remove`. Several changes to one row between two cursors answer once, as the row is now. A cursor never expires: the store keeps a removed row's version, item and change order (`ns_gone`). `wait: true` holds the call when nothing changed after `after`, until a change arrives or the call's own time (settings.json `call_seconds`) ends, then answers what there is, so a device learns of a change without a timer of its own. show_item {item, device?} answers the live name or folder holding that item now, or not found. Pins: a pin rule is a row of the person's own (`pin_rules.scope`): {id, device, items, label?, on?}. `device` names the device it applies to (whatever id the device's shell gives itself) and `items` the items it keeps on that device: a file's item keeps the file, a folder's item keeps everything under it, and since an item never changes the pin follows a rename or a move, as a file browser's own pin does. set_pin_rule {id, device, items, label?, on?, expected_version} and remove_pin_rule {id, expected_version} write one rule at the version read (0 for a new rule); list_pin_rules {device?, after?, limit?} reads them. list_files, show_item and list_changes asked with `device` answer `kept` on each name: true when an `on` rule of that device names the name's item or the item of a folder it is under. thumbnail {name_or_identity, size} answers {identity, size, media_type, content_base64} for a picture of the file at most `size` pixels on its longer edge, or {identity, size, thumbnail: null, reason} when no maker takes the file's media type: made once by the first maker of `thumbnails.makers` whose media type prefix the file's media type starts with (the program reads the file by range from a one-request-at-a-time loopback address the call opens for it and closes when it ends), and kept as the file's result of kind `thumbnails.result_kind` under its content identity, one field per size, so a changed file is a new identity and a thumbnail is never stale. make_folder {name, expected_version} makes one folder in a folder that exists (0: nothing is at that name now) and answers its row {kind: folder, name, item, version, generation}; a name or folder already there is a conflict. bounds {} answers the numbers a caller sizes its calls by, read from where each is kept, so no client keeps a copy: list_default and list_most (names a page answers by default and at most), read_most (bytes read_file answers at most), span_most (bytes read_file_span answers at most, one stored range), chunk_bytes (the most one stored chunk holds; aligned reads waste least), write_most (bytes write_file keeps in one call), piece_most (bytes one write_file_piece carries at most). A refusal is {code, outcome: not_started | unknown, detail?}; the store's compare-and-set refusal is `namespace_conflict` with outcome not_started (nothing changed), never an outage. Compare-and-set: write_file, write_file_start, move_names, set_aside and put_back take `expected_version`, the version of the name (or of the folder, for a folder) the caller read; the store's one write of that row is made only at that version (src/store `mutate`), so a name changed by someone else since it was read is refused with a conflict and nothing of it changes. write_file_start keeps it as the upload's name version, so write_file_finish names the same version. The WebDAV folder's If-Match passes the version it read the same way.
